Some are simultaneous hermaphrodites, which can produce both eggs and sperm at the same time. Others are sequential hermaphrodites, in which the eggs and sperm mature at different times.

The difference in this study, published in Current Biology, was the length of time taken to get to the conclusion that sexual differentiation doesn't happen until all of a species' genetic material has been expressed. The researchers got that estimate from comparing an animal's genes in the form of its skin cells to others that had been preserved in the sediment in order to reveal how long since different animals started to diverge.

The skin morph, or form, of these particular organisms, once they're dead, can last more than a million years. As for species that are hermaphrodites, these animals are also genetically identical, but have a single copy of each chromosome. Ctenophora (/tᵻˈnɒfərə/; singular ctenophore, /ˈtɛnəfɔːr/ or /ˈtiːnəfɔːr/; from the Greek κτείς kteis 'comb' and φέρω pherō 'carry'; commonly known as comb jellies) is a phylum of animals that live in marine waters worldwide. They are closely related to jellyfish, corals, and sea stars, but unlike many of these other 'jelly' animals, they do not possess a skeleton or any other internal organs. The only internal organs found inside ctenophores are cilia, spiracles, and mouth parts that work together to secrete a sticky secretion. They have long, filamentous digestive systems that are capable of absorbing and digesting algae. They also form large colonies in the reef where they live.

Ctenophores are important in the coral reef ecosystem because they are responsible for filtering out many harmful nutrients. If the water is polluted, high concentrations of phytoplankton (algae) produce harmful waste products such as polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), the major component of PCBs in sea water, that can easily harm corals. Ctenophores filter out contaminants and remove them from the water. On their own, however, the removal of pollution is not enough to restore the coral reef environment to a balanced state. To correct these environmental issues, researchers need to improve corals' ability to produce and absorb these key components, which in turn would increase the reef's ability to grow in response to the changes in the environment.

Ctenophores are one of three families of reef microorganisms that comprise the macrozooplankton (Mozoplankton).

From the Eocene onwards, the ongoing Alpine orogeny caused a N–S rift system to develop in this zone. The main elements of this rift are the Upper Rhine Graben, in southwest Germany and eastern France and the Lower Rhine Embayment, in northwest Germany and the southeastern Netherlands. By the time of the Miocene, a river system had developed in the Upper Rhine Graben, that continued northward and is considered the first Rhine river. The Lower Rhine Embayment, consisting of a few smaller rivers (including the Rhine), was largely underlain by dacitic volcanism during the Triassic Period, with the Upper Rhine Embayment beginning to develop during the Early Jurassic. By the beginning of the Eocene, a line of erosion had developed from the Middle East and into Europe, starting at the southernmost part of the Lower Rhine and extending into Germany and later northern France with the beginning of the Jurassic. The eastern and western parts of the Eocene continental margin, however, are still largely underlain by the Upper Rhine Embayment with only a few minor dacitic blocks.

Facial Features – During the Eocene, most of the German coast appeared to have had a thick sea to sand layer, the Upper Rhine, which had been formed during the Maastrichtian Oligocene when sea-level was still significantly elevated (1–4 m). The Rhine Embayment was made of numerous dendritic structures (flutes, canals, and river channels) which had been eroded during the Maastrichtian Oligocene. In Japan, at the end of the Asuka period (538–710) and the early Nara period (710–794), the men who fulfilled roles similar to those of modern pharmacists were highly respected. The place of pharmacists in society was expressly defined in the Taihō Code (701) and re-stated in the Yōrō Code (718). Ranked positions in the pre-Heian Imperial court were established; and this organizational structure remained largely intact until the Meiji Restoration (1868). The positions of pharmacist and physician combined a set of duties. They served in all branches of the prefecture's functions and received various emoluments. They also worked at hospitals (see Yōji-in and Kyōin-in) as well as in the fields of medicine, surgery, and pharmacy.

Although physicians and pharmacists were involved in health care and medicine, they were not doctors. The profession of medicine in pre-Heian Japan consisted of "tōjin" (pharmacy) and "tōkai" (medicine), each specialized in a particular area of human health. The former's tasks included the preparation of medicines, their administration, and the monitoring of their effects on the body by means of observations (tōjin). The latter's responsibilities included the diagnosis, treatment, and surveillance of infectious diseases and the detection and diagnosis of maladies of the human body. Both tōjin and tōkai had a responsibility toward their patients; patients were considered to be their "clients."

According to the Code, pharmacists were responsible for controlling the circulation of medicines from pharmacy and pharmacy shops to the hospitals. Oxygen storage equipment and services are not often available for use by other groups of personnel, such as emergency medical professionals.

Trioxygen (O 3) is usually known as ozone and is a very reactive allotrope of oxygen that is damaging to lung tissue. Ozone is produced in the upper atmosphere when O 2 combines with atomic oxygen made by the splitting of O 2 by ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Since ozone absorbs strongly in the UV region of the spectrum, the ozone layer of the upper atmosphere functions as a protective radiation shield for the planet.

The ozone layer is one hundred times thicker than the Earth's atmosphere. It covers almost the entire surface of the Earth and protects organisms on the surface. In less than 24 hours of exposure to ozone, the ozone layer can be reduced by 50% to 100%. Human beings can tolerate just a third of the initial ozone layer protection of the planet, but an intense UV ray of 150 nm or more can reduce the protective ozone layer to 15-25% compared on a daily basis to that of the Earth's troposphere (the layer of atmosphere where most of the Earth's clouds are).

The protection of the ozone layer depends on the thickness (in meters, not inches) and duration of the UV-absorbing ozone species. When the thickness of the ozone layer is less than 6-16 meters (20-40 miles or 25-50 kilometers), the ozone is completely destroyed (called a "polar stratospheric hole"). On the other hand, when the ozone is over 15 meters (50-80 miles) thick, the ozone layer is able to protect the Earth for a period of time. Scientists and modelers have been searching for methods and mechanisms to create holes in the ozone due to increase or decrease of ultraviolet radiation.

With two-cylinder compounds used in railway work, the pistons are connected to the cranks as with a two-cylinder simple at 90° out of phase with each other (quartered). When the double expansion group is duplicated, producing a 4-cylinder compound, the individual pistons within the group are usually balanced at 180°, the groups being set at 90° to each other. In one case (the first type of Vauclain compound), the pistons worked in the same phase driving a common crosshead and crank, again set at 90° as for a two-cylinder engine. This arrangement allowed it to be used in some locomotives with 2 (2½-horsepower) cylinders, and hence still produce a higher output because of the additional power put into the crankshaft's rotation. The crankshaft was then turned to make the Vauclain compound. By this process the cylinder head angle increased. With a two-cylinder Vauclain compound, the crank's rotation was driven by the power of the cylinder at one end, while the cylinder at the other end turned the crankshaft making the compound.


The crank is only a portion of the crankcase, and for very large engines the whole crankcase would be made of iron due to the high carbon content. The iron case needed to be designed to cope with the high combustion requirements of a large cylinder, and the use of a lower carbon content case made more of a profit.


A single stroke cylinder used to run a larger engine had a cylindrical bore which became gradually broader as the stroke grew. Following the utilitarian principle of seeking the greatest good for the greatest number – economic inequality is problematic. John Dalton's original atomic hypothesis assumed that all elements were monatomic and that the atoms in compounds would normally have the simplest atomic ratios with respect to one another. For example, Dalton assumed that water's formula was HO, giving the atomic mass of oxygen as 8 times that of hydrogen, instead of the modern value of about 16. He realized though that in some compounds, the ionic hydrogen could be substituted with a lighter or even heavier one using the chemical bond. A specific example of this is carbon-12, which exists in many compounds, some containing carbon, but most containing carbon-12. By substituting carbon-12 with a heavier element it is possible to change the atomic number of the carbon atom, thus changing the atomic structure.

Hydrogen is the lightest element, so the hydrogen atoms should be the simplest and most mobile. This hypothesis for all the elements is called the pure theory.

Dalton concluded that there is only one simple way to make all the elements from hydrogen: by putting hydrogen and deuterium together in a nuclear reactor. Only then would the ratio of hydrogen-3 to hydrogen-15 be zero, and then the elements could be produced. This isotopic "split" of Hydrogen is usually referred to as the "nuclear" hypothesis. This hypothesis is based on the fact that deuterium is unstable so it has the potential to split into deuterium-23 (23 protons and 23 neutrons) and protons (24 neutrons) when irradiated. In contrast, hydrogen itself has a very long half-life, so it would have no chance to split into an isotope other than the stable isotope hydrogen-4, which would have a mass of about 1.007 g.

The air pressure in the boiler can be regulated either using a valve regulated air pump or air-driven valves to a valve regulated electric pump. In some cases, the boiler heat exchanger may be the only source of the air pressure required for the boiler. From there, the lake steadily increased in size until it reached a level approximately twice the area of the state of Delaware. The rise in water levels caused erosion to develop on the lake bed. During this period, the lake gradually became much less flat. As the lake's shoreline continued to decline, the lake became increasingly turbulent. It was also during this time that the Rhone River Valley and Lake Constance became separated for the first time since prehistoric times.

endogenous endophthalmitis is a rare and severe intraocular infection which can be vision - threatening .

A single case of endophthalmitis from the eyes of a woman in her 40's was reported at the time of this update. She had acute endophthalmitis that required systemic antibiotic treatment, and she subsequently received a corneal graft reconstruction to correct her vision loss. An eye-coloured staining, sometimes seen in corneal and/or iris biopsies of endophthalmitis, may be associated with mycobacteria, including species of Mycobacterium tuberculosum, Mycobacterium avium subspecies evanescens (T. avium) and Mycobacterium kansasii. The organisms may be present in a similar way to streptococci found in endophthalmitis and may be identified by positive Gram staining on eye biopsy or through conventional Gram stain. However, the Gram staining of pathobiologic species is less specific than the culture methods used for other bacteria associated with endophthalmitis.

Clinicians treating patients with endophthalmitis are reminded to consider endophthalmitis as an important problem requiring ongoing management and to follow current national guidelines for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients with endophthalmitis.

French Huguenots made two attempts to establish a haven in North America. In 1562, naval officer Jean Ribault led an expedition that explored Florida and the present-day Southeastern U.S., and founded the outpost of Charlesfort on Parris Island, South Carolina. The Wars of Religion precluded a return voyage, and the outpost was abandoned.

In 1581, four French Huguenots and two Spanish colonials arrived at Port Royal, Texas, in what was then a part of the Spanish colony of Ojinaga. The initial settlement was unsuccessful; the colonists left on October 5 as they could not agree on a common religious practice. As the group sailed back to Spain under captain Juan de Escalante, three of them were drowned near the island of Baja California; Escalante and the other surviving colonists fled to Spain in panic.

After a period of time, Spanish forces defeated their Indian enemies in 1718, and the Spanish crown granted them land on which to settle. One of the first colonists, named Samuel de Leon, traveled from Philadelphia, Pa. to the Virgin Islands; his descendants are still living in San Antonio. Another pioneer, named Rafael, moved the community from the Virgin Islands to the present-day state of Louisiana.

By the late nineteenth century, two distinct Christian-based communities had developed in the Virgin Islands—one composed mostly of Native Americans, while the other, also made up of Native Americans and English, is primarily Hispanic. In the aftermath of American annexation, the Virgin Islands government adopted a policy of assimilating many Native American settlers, giving a new Native American name, the San Ildefonso Pueblo (the New San Ildefonso Nation), and assimilating them to the native population of the islands, often including children.

dentigerous cysts are the most common type of developmental odontogenic cysts arising from the crowns of impacted , embedded , or unerupted teeth . The most common types of lesions of this type are benign (eg, granulomatous lesions); they are extremely benign (eg, no evidence of bone loss) and most often are benign and noninflammatory. Sometimes, however, these lesions progress to a more serious stage that may lead to the emergence of lesions that are more invasive and can potentially cause serious deformity of the dentition. These lesions are often associated with an abscess or abscessed tooth or abscess/denture of an underlying periodontal lesion. The majority of these affected teeth are the roots of permanent dentition.

Although clinical, anatomic, and pathological findings may differ from those described above, cysts of the upper portion of dental arch and crown are often associated with a variety of nonspecific pain factors including swelling, tenderness, tooth pain, and decreased dental enjoyment. They may also cause a decreased sense of taste and taste buds in the tongue, which may cause nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. The cysts often do not appear until several months or even a year after the root canal.

They only pupate and then emerge from their burrows after 7, 13 or 17 years, at which point they fly about, breed, and then die after a few weeks at most.

By analyzing the positions of the twigs on the body of a Magicicada larva, biologists discovered that it makes no use of the prime numbers for calculating the correct position of the head and body, or for guiding food intake into their mouth. When a caterpillar digs it burrow, the end of the burrow is always a single twig, allowing for the use of prime numbers to calculate the appropriate point of entry into the burrow.

The most likely reason for the lack of prime numbers in the cicada brain is that the larvae have no control over the timing of their burrowing. A caterpillar that burrowed right before a particular twig is fully developed would be eating it right after that twig, because the twig is a waste product. Similarly, a caterpillar that burrowed next to the next twig would need to eat before it emerged, and since it doesn't feed before pupating, it'll get eaten when it emerges.

When the caterpillar emerges, though, one, two, or three of its eggs will be still clinging to the twig, and the larvae will use them for food. The problem is that the caterpillar will still have twigs wrapped up on its body, so it'll be unable to take the first, second, or second-to-last twig. This will cause the larvae to leave their burrows, thus allowing the burrow to empty of food before the caterpillar emerges.

One of the more notable applications of printing technology was the chao, the paper money of the Yuan. In addition to serving as legal tender in China, chao had a number of other purposes, including protecting commerce, maintaining law and order, and issuing money without inflation due to its value being pegged to the dollar. It was a successful currency throughout the empire, especially in the east.

Chinese printing presses were most widespread east of the Yellow River. It is unknown when the printing was introduced to China, but as early as 500 AD, China had a number of these "universal" or "universal" banks with an unlimited capacity to issue circulating notes. Later, these banks also issued the coins and deposits required for merchants to conduct business.

In the adult anesthesiologist, during a pediatric auscultation, the most common clinical findings tend to revolve around the neck and facial features related to airway occlusion, especially a facial hypoplasia, a wide palate, and a cleft palate. These findings may be more difficult to identify during an airway assessment by the pediatric anesthesiologist.


In the pediatric anesthesiologist, airway management is a challenging problem since the anatomy is different between adult and pediatric patients and the conditions underlying a congenital occlusive airway are unique.


During an auscultation of a pediatric ear, nose, and throat patient, airway management can be complex and challenging. The airway may be closed by means of an endotracheal tube or may be open and unresponsive to tracheal intubation. In pediatric patients, many surgical procedures, such as craniotomy, cricothyrotomy, and tracheostomy are performed to provide access to tracheal and bronchi.


As the anesthesiologist, it is important to understand the different conditions for which pediatric anesthesiologists have access to the pediatric airway, as well as their unique anatomy. It is also important to understand the differences between anesthetic techniques used in pediatric patients.

It uses a property of all noncommutative (and nonnegative) groups where the probability of the group expanding into its own superset is the product of all permutations of the group elements. In this case, the probability of a group expanding to its own superset is the product of all the permutations of the original elements. In animals with systemic lupus erythematosus or SLE, the inflammatory process precedes or follows the clinical onset of disease, or early onset of disease. Macrophages are the primary source of the eicosanoid prostaglandins C2, C3, and C4 in lupus. C2 and C3 may stimulate production of TNF, whereas C4 may inhibit production. The capabilities approach – sometimes called the human development approach – looks at income inequality and poverty as form of “capability deprivation”. Unlike neoliberalism, which “defines well-being as utility maximization”, economic growth and income are considered a means to an end rather than the end itself. Its goal is to “wid[en] people’s choices and the level of their achieved well-being” through increasing functionings (the things a person values doing), capabilities (the freedom to enjoy functionings) and agency (the ability to pursue valued goals).

According to the capabilities approach, poor individuals are not deprived of choice, however they are deprived of choices based on their actual (rather than projected) capabilities relative to other choices available.

Eliminating barriers to a basic income guarantee is not economic growth that benefits only the rich.

This includes both the loss of income from work and any barriers to economic growth such as a reduction in productivity or economic growth. It also includes some form of tax increase which, for example, is often put forward as a way to offset the basic income. (In reality, it would more likely cost more than offset the basic income as the basic income guarantee is not "tax free" at all.)

A Universal Basic Income is a much better way of tackling poverty than some austerity measures.

Universal, universal income is the most fair way to tackle poverty. It would not be only better at reducing poverty, but would also more likely lift the economy, thereby providing relief for everyone. At this stage, the benefits of such a measure are uncertain and will only be known once more evidence is collected on the specific effectiveness of a Universal Basic Income.

The Normans (Norman: Nourmands; French: Normands; Latin: Normanni) were the people who in the 10th and 11th centuries gave their name to Normandy, a region in France. They lived in a predominantly Celtic style of dress, lived in mountainous areas, and, generally speaking, preferred to keep their distance from Rome.


Their name comes from a Celtic word meaning "of the sky".


Although they were, on occasion, involved in fierce tribal conflicts with their neighbours, they were not known as the "Vikings" by anyone but other inhabitants in the West.


The Normans came to rule the area between the Rhine and Seine Rivers beginning in the 8th century.


Their territory included what is now France. Later, in the 10th century, the country came to be known as the Anglo-Saxon Kingdom of the Franks in Northern France.


Although this period was largely prosperous, and their empire, however limited, extended over modern France and parts of Belgium, the name "Normans" is now primarily used to describe people who lived in Britain during (and following) the period known as "The Norman Conquest".

A natural number greater than 1 that is not a prime number is called a composite number. For example, 5 is prime because 1 and 5 are its only positive integer factors, whereas 6 is composite because it has the divisors 2 and 3 in addition to 1 and 6.

Note: It is common to see numbers ranging in size from 5 through 20 or even up to 100,000,000. These numbers are also composite, as they represent a finite set of prime numbers with the same divisors.

Composite numbers cannot be divided to produce distinct results.

Let the number n be the product of 2 and 3. The largest possible n is 3, so n is composite. However, 2 cannot be divided to produce the smallest possible n, 0. All composite numbers include some remainder, and n itself may be the product of two such remainder numbers.

A natural number with no remainder (or a composite number itself) has no divisors other than itself.

Often having an elementary formulation, many of these conjectures have withstood a proof for decades: all four of Landau's problems from 1912 are still unsolved. One of them is Goldbach's conjecture, which asserts that every even integer n greater than 2 can be written as a sum of two primes. Another is the so-called D'Alembert conjecture, asserting the existence of a prime number, P, the unique factor of one. Of all the prime conjectures in mathematics, however, few are as hard to prove as the Riemann hypothesis.

It is not a trivial problem to prove an equation that involves an infinite series of primes. Consider the simple example of P = 2. The simplest way to prove this was proposed by the Swiss mathematician Georg Cantor in 1782 as a solution to the cubic equation of the natural logarithm. However, it proves too hard for the typical mathematician, even much later (e.g., in 1930 by Cantor).

The general problem is not so hard if you also have a good understanding of calculus, but not in case of many-valued calculus. An oscillating cylinder steam engine is a variant of the simple expansion steam engine which does not require valves to direct steam into and out of the cylinder. Instead of valves, the entire cylinder rocks, or oscillates, such that one or more holes in the cylinder line up with holes in a fixed port face or in the pivot mounting (trunnion). A rotating piston drives a shaft into the oscillating cylinder or a rotary plunger pushes the piston into the fixed port, the shaft or pivoting plungers moving the piston within the cylinder while the rotary plunger pushes the piston back out. The steam is then blown from the rotating cylinder via a condenser (the steam is cooled off in the boiler before getting to this point). The steam and the heated water are then passed across the steam-generating steam pipes, and the warm water is used to wash a variety of things, making it a useful power plant.

The basic principle of the oscillatory steam engine is the same as in the simple expansion steam engine, except that the moving portions of the engine rotates at a different rate (due to an alternator). The alternator is the moving part of any steam energy system. The alternator is an electromagnet which turns at about 200 revs (1000 Hz). The steam and electrical power may then be supplied by steam turbines, to the steam condenser, water boiler, or other power plants, in the same way they are supplied by the simple steam engines. The simple steam engines are usually referred to as "compressor and turbine steam engines," because all the steam is first converted into steam by compressing a piston, which is driven into the cylinder by a reciprocating part. Generally treated in a lightweight vein though not lacking in certain moments which might be called dramatic, the series would seem to be aimed at people of around fifty who can rember those times, as, it should be stated, anyone younger either chooses to ignore such happenings or is busily occupied in other things.

The best thing that can be said of this series is Ana Duato's rôle as mother of three children: she plays the part of the total housewife of the times really well, manifesting that peculiar Spanish penchant, especially noticeable among women, of letting all her thinking and her doings be carried forward by the impetus of her heart, without any resorting to the use of the brain. As we say in Spain, common sense is one of the least common senses. She is, however, not much of a character and she is never given too much to do, so it would appear that she is being exploited here by the director's good nature. Still, she has a certain charm, the way she plays out all the parts that her children are supposed to act out with her is really touching.

Of course, for other people, some might say, it can be a bit tiresome or tiresomely sentimental, but it is not a bad series, if that's what you have in mind.

The shape of the Rhine delta is determined by two bifurcations: first, at Millingen aan de Rijn, the Rhine splits into Waal and Pannerdens Kanaal, which changes its name to Nederrijn at Angeren, and second near Arnhem, the IJssel branches off from the Nederrijn. This creates three main flows, two of which change names rather often. The largest and southern main branch begins as Waal and continues as Boven Merwede ("Upper Merwede"), Beneden Merwede ("Lower Merwede"), Noord River ("North River"), Nieuwe Maas ("New Meuse"), Het Scheur ("the Rip") and Nieuwe Waterweg ("New Waterway"). The second, older, main branch of the Rhine in the North flows down to the IJssel while the IJssel branch flows down to the Het Scheur.

The riverfront between the two main branches is marked with the "Achtswerk der Verbraucher" ("Arts of the Weaver") sign and the canal bank. The IJssel crosses the Danube via a bridge at Arnhem, and runs in a channel between the river Rhine and the Nelen river, known as West Rijn. This part of the river can be quite a wild place. During the winter months, the Rijn is an attractive place for skaters but, for the most part, it stays dry and empty at that time of the year.

To further highlight the difference between a problem and an instance, consider the following instance of the decision version of the traveling salesman problem: Is there a route of at most 2000 kilometres passing through all of Germany's 15 largest cities? The quantitative answer to this particular problem instance is of little use for solving other instances of the problem, such as asking for a round trip through all sites in Milan whose total length is at most 10 km. In all these situations, the example from which the quantitative results are derived is not an instance of the traveling salesman problem itself. Instead, it is a different problem instance that has nothing to do with the traveling salesman problem: A traveller travels by bus between Vienna and Prague, which has an arrival route of about 4000 km and a return route of about 1200 km to Amsterdam.

This distinction between problems and instances is at the heart of the idea of "algorithmic differences of opinion" of Wittgenstein, and it is the idea that underpins the work of a number of "deep learning" researchers, including Stuart Russell, Andrew Ng, Yoshua Bengio and Bengio, et al. Two of the primary methods for identifying rocks in the laboratory are through optical microscopy and by using an electron microprobe. In an optical mineralogy analysis, thin sections of rock samples are analyzed through a petrographic microscope, where the minerals can be identified through their different properties in plane-polarized and cross-polarized light, including their birefringence, pleochroism, twinning, and interference properties with a conoscopic lens. As a mineralogical technique, electron microprobe detection can identify minerals by identifying chemical signals that exist in rock matrix at discrete points on the rock surface. These chemical signals can be identified either directly or indirectly through their correlation with the properties of other minerals. The process is similar to that where the chemical composition of a rock is analyzed by a spectroscope, but instead of a chemical composition of an atomic ion being determined, the compound is analyzed by the chemical composition of its component atoms.

Rock Types Rock types are also widely defined by geological characteristics. The classification by rock type is based on two geologic features: the presence of lithification and the presence of sedimentary rocks. Lithification refers to the presence of fossilized limestone and shale layers (e.g., the Appalachian basin and the Rocky mountains), which form a solid or broken pile, and are usually interpreted as having formed at a higher elevation and thus contain a greater density of minerals. Sedimentary rocks consist of a mixture of rocks with differing chemical compositions, each of which is preserved as an individual rock component (e.g., sandstone, limestone, shale, etc.). In the process of rock mineral accumulation, certain rock types accumulate over, or beneath, another. These two types of rock types are separated in the rock strata by a chemical or physical barrier. Although these two types of rock layers are often used to distinguish rock types, this is not an all-encompassing class. Rock-forming processes affect all rock types, which are also affected by the physical and chemical environment. This means that, although lithification is a primary rock type criterion for geologic interpretation, the rock layers are not always a good indicator of the rock type.

Economist Simon Kuznets argued that levels of economic inequality are in large part the result of stages of development. According to Kuznets, countries with low levels of development have relatively equal distributions of wealth. As a country develops, it acquires more capital, which leads to the owners of this capital having more wealth and income and introducing inequality.

However, the evidence suggests that this idea may not be entirely true. The research also suggests that, in some situations, inequality can be good.

A study by economists Angus Deaton and Anne Case of Princeton University, published in 2014, provided empirical evidence that inequality of income over periods of 10 to 20 years is related to levels of longevity – the longer a person lives, the lower their probability of dying at a younger age, due to lower mortality rates for each succeeding year of life.

How to measure inequality

Although there are many ways in which the gap between rich and poor can be measured, it is perhaps most widely used in relation to wealth, which relates to disposable income: income of households that is not subject to tax.

In other words, some measure of wealth can be used to measure the extent to which a group of people controls resources and income. For example, the wealth of an individual can be defined as the total value of their assets, including their assets, and their debt – which includes their mortgages and other debts.

GDP is the broadest measure of economic activity available. GDP measures the value of the economy, calculated as income and value added (also called'spending') plus net exports.

Other widely used income measures include the share (or the income) the poorest fifth of households receive on average, and the share of income received by the richest fifth of households.

Poverty measures are a specific measure of the level of deprivation and inactivity, defined as people not being working or actively seeking employment.

Each year, the southern California area has about 10,000 earthquakes. Nearly all of them are so small that they are not felt. Only several hundred are greater than magnitude 3.0, and only about 15–20 are greater than magnitude 4.0. But even a relatively small earthquake can have seismic consequences around the globe, as in the case of the 2010 Loma Prieta earthquake, which devastated parts of the San Francisco Bay Area in May 2010.

"We can't put our finger on why this is, but I suspect we'll find one of the largest mysteries because it has affected, directly and indirectly, more than a dozen countries, including Australia, New Zealand, Chile and Peru -- and there haven't been any major earthquakes," says John Vidale, a seismologist at the University of Oklahoma.

Why the earthquakes are happening in California is less clear, and even less certain. Several factors could be at work, including quakes in the nearby deep sea floor, changes in the continental crust, and the release of carbon dioxide from the melting of the ice sheets covering the West Antarctic ice sheet. In addition to these, scientists have been trying to understand the links between wastewater injection and increased earthquake activity.

"This study adds further uncertainty to this whole issue," says David Carlson, a volcanologist at the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) in Menlo PARK, Calif.

The Rankine cycle is sometimes referred to as a practical Carnot cycle because, when an efficient turbine is used, the TS diagram begins to resemble the Carnot cycle. The Carnot cycle has two important limits on the work per unit area, which is the ratio of area to the work that can be done.

If the work per unit area in a turbine can be reduced to a near limit, then the work per unit area can be increased. This will allow the turbine to spin faster or for a larger area.

If the work per unit area is always the same, then increasing efficiency through lower power requirements and increasing the area of the cycle will lead to bigger, faster, more efficient turbines. As a rule of thumb, larger turbines will be more efficient than small turbines (in terms of unit of energy produced).

As in a practical Carnot cycle, most turbines are in the first of the two quadrants of the Rankine scale. The top turbine on the right has a power rating of 20GW, and about the same size in area as a house. From the death of Augustus in AD 14 until after AD 70, Rome accepted as her Germanic frontier the water-boundary of the Rhine and upper Danube. Beyond these rivers she held only the fertile plain of Frankfurt, opposite the Roman border fortress of Moguntiacum (Mainz), the southernmost slopes of the Black Forest and a few scattered bridge-heads. The northern section of this frontier, where the Rhine is deep and broad, remained the Roman boundary until the empire fell.

Rome did not have as large a population as the Germanic tribes. Her total population was only three million in her peak and had steadily decreased from the 1.5 million in her early history. Most were low-caste German peasants but there were also several high-caste, mostly upper-class Roman colonists. The Roman population increased as much as 10% in the fourth century, the early fourth century, and continued to rise into the fifth century. But for political reasons, the empire was divided into districts (states) by about the fourth century. In this way Rome was able to deal effectively with the border disputes of a rapidly expanding German state in the north of the empire.

The city of Rome developed rapidly through the fourth of the six centuries into one of the great world centres of classical culture. The cities of Milan and Byzantium were then rapidly surpassed by Rome.

Since its founding, the EU has operated among an increasing plurality of national and globalising legal systems. This has meant both the European Court of Justice and the highest national courts have had to develop principles to resolve conflicts of laws between different systems. Within the EU itself, the Court of Justice's view is that if EU law conflicts with a provision of national law, then EU law has primacy. Under certain circumstances, the Court also allows the EU to set out 'a different legal standard' for the application of EU law to member states - usually on a case by case basis.

The European Court's view on conflict has not extended as far as to establish 'new' rights. This is in part because courts within the EU will take into account their own laws when interpreting the EU treaties and national constitutions, and the Court has not had to consider whether new rights might arise as a result. Instead, the ECJ has applied the same principle - that both national and EU law should consider whether a given measure could be justified by a valid overriding interest for the individual state or person concerned.

For example, if there was a case to review whether EU citizenship rights and obligations should be available to non-EU citizens, the Court would be likely to regard those rights as part of the common law of the EU as a whole.

In line with this principle, the Court has considered rights arising under EU law such as financial aid for the poorer regions of the EU.

Report P-2626 described a general architecture for a large-scale, distributed, survivable communications network.

It described a network which could be self-healing as well as self-preserving, meaning that there were no catastrophic failures. As the B-265 system became aware of a fault in communications, it would automatically self-patching the faulty connection; the message would continue to be delivered to the client, only to be lost on reboot. Similarly, if the network was attacked, the attacker would be unable to recover the communication, requiring the attacker to reboot the network.

For a distributed adaptive message block switching network, a message must contain at least one block of information—a header with the source, destination, and destination port numbers. The message block would include a checksum field and an acknowledgement field. After receiving a message-block, the network would scan the block and perform one of its two operations: either accept the message and return the message as part of the next block from an external source or discard the entire message block—and forward it—to the next client. Upon determining whether the blocks could be merged without changing the message content and header checksum, packet routing would be performed to ensure that all the messages would be processed. These problems can happen particularly with public projects, where the availability of funds varies considerably across the country.

However, while public projects will not necessarily fail to meet their costs, the risk of failure rises dramatically in public-private partnerships (PPPs). Under PPPs, the public sector, in general, pays for the project. However for some public projects, the private sector will have to be involved, to provide the infrastructure and management services, for example, water and sewerage. PPPs also have greater risks associated with them with regard to project delivery and financing, and have less flexibility for financing, as the Government will still have to meet its financial obligations.

In the United Kingdom, the basic principle is that Parliament, as the sovereign expression of democratic legitimacy, can decide whether it wishes to expressly legislate against EU law. This, however, would only happen in the case of an express wish of the people to withdraw from the EU. In other words, in the United Kingdom, the people can take their own views on the law in question in a democratic fashion, and can also decide, explicitly or implicitly, to opt out (through a referendum). (a)that reference was a reference to a law of the United Kingdom, or

(b)that reference was a reference to a law of a Member State of the European Union,

that provision were a reference to a law of a Member State of the European Union (a reference to an expression of European Community law being treated as referring to any law of that State)." (emphasis added)

Although it was a debit card, Bank of America's new product wasn't debit for debit card purposes. It would allow you to purchase goods and services. The company advertised it as a "universal payment card."

BankAmericard was originally intended to be used at local stores and over the telephone. But just as quickly as it started becoming popular, it was abandoned by retailers. After all, debit cards are very easy and convenient to use, but they don't really allow customers to buy goods and services using their own money. And there's no way around paying fees with the card once a transaction is established.

Fast forward to May 6, 1964. Back then, an American Express card was also considered "universal payment." But that didn't help it gain wide acceptance -- and Bank of America didn't get to market with it until October 1966.

Geologists use a number of field, laboratory, and numerical modeling methods to decipher Earth history and understand the processes that occur on and inside the Earth. In typical geological investigations, geologists use primary information related to petrology (the study of rocks), stratigraphy (the study of sedimentary layers), and structural geology (the study of positions of rock units and their deformation). In many cases, geologists also study modern soils, rivers, landscapes, and glaciers; investigate past and current life and biogeochemical pathways, and use geophysical methods to investigate the subsurface. In some cases, geological field schools or undergraduate undergraduate programs may be employed.

How Is Geology Researched By Professional Geologists?

Professional geologists use science-based techniques to identify and resolve geological processes during investigations. These techniques can be performed in a number of ways, such as by observing the results of tests done in a laboratory or on a computer; testing geologic formations in the laboratory or on a computer; or observing the effects of laboratory tests on sample rock, mineral, or other samples.

Professional geologists can also use a variety of computer-based analytical testing, often with reference to a primary source of basic rock properties like permeability or resistance to earthquakes. Also, professional geologists are often able to obtain a knowledge of local and regional geological and geological hazards, and can formulate strategies to mitigate these risks. The graph isomorphism problem, the discrete logarithm problem and the integer factorization problem are examples of problems believed to be NP-intermediate. The general case is shown by the diagonalization problem.

Ladner constructed a new model of NP-completeness of the form P = NP-hard and used it to construct a simple example: finding the shortest distance between two points. His analysis shows that the shortest distance is P - P. Since there are many paths between two points, the shortest path must be the shortest. P - P was proved to be unprovable by an NP-complete machine. However, according to the model of P - P, finding it would necessarily require solving a NP problem. Now that you have an overview of the film - my advice for a viewer is as follows: Get the DVD. While you wait, watch the movie again. Just like an opera, the movie gets better as it's rewatched. If you've already seen your copy of the film - go back and watch it in a mirror. Because Vonnegut was a self-aware creative, you will notice certain cinematic touches that are unlike the director's actual film. You will notice the dialogue being narrated by one character rather than the other, or a shot switching between past and present tense, a moment of silence that may be the exact moment when you realize something was going to happen later. These little details help to immerse you in the film, and help to remind you of all the things it could have been.

Charles W. Eliot, president 1869–1909, eliminated the favored position of Christianity from the curriculum while opening it to student self-direction. Derived from William Ellery Channing and Ralph Waldo Emerson, these convictions were focused on the dignity and worth of human nature, the right and ability of each person to perceive truth, and the indwelling God in each person. For these reasons, Eliot's idea of the secularized university was deeply rooted in traditional Unitarian beliefs. "The ideal man," Eliot said, "is a free spirit who believes in himself, a moral teacher, a lover of life, and of all that is good," and a "perfect student, who studies for a better man, and learns to love himself." Eliot's education philosophy made the distinction between the university for the privileged and for the masses.

Most of the Rhine's current course was not under the ice during the last Ice Age; although, its source must still have been a glacier. A tundra, with Ice Age flora and fauna, stretched across middle Europe, from Asia to the Atlantic Ocean. The Rhine was then, as it is now -- the river is its main valley -- a very big river. The Rhine rose gradually from the Baltic to the lowlands of Central Europe then fell south into Northern Spain. As a flood-tide, the Rhine entered into the Strait of Gibraltar, between Africa and Europe. It crossed the Mediterranean. During the following decades, the Rhine was slowly transformed as a stream of salt, due to melting glaciers. The sea rose, and the Rhine was drained by the Jordan River and the O.E. Gulf of Suez. During the first Ice Age, the Rhine was a major river of salt, a very ancient but still effective means of flood control over a large area.

The Rhine, which runs along the northern flank of the Alpine Alps, passes through the countries of the European Union. It flows along the German border on the north and near the border of France on the south, and it comes close to the city of Munich in the south. European Union law is a body of treaties and legislation, such as Regulations and Directives, which have direct effect or indirect effect on the laws of European Union member states. The three sources of European Union law are primary law, secondary law and supplementary law. The main sources of primary law are the Treaties establishing the European Union. The main sources of secondary law include the laws of each member state of the EU. The three main sources of supplementary law are the agreements governing the EU's single market and customs union.

The EU's primary law is composed of legal acts, including treaties. Each treaty contains provisions on the substance of EU law and on certain substantive matters. However, the Treaty establishing the EU does not have a separate charter of fundamental rights. Some treaties may be amended or repealed by another treaty, which in turn is subject to approval by the ordinary legislative procedure in each member state. The EU law thus consists mainly of texts which derive from the principal texts of the Treaty establishing the EU. The EU laws may be referred to as the constitutional laws of the Union. EU laws can be changed by both federal and member state legislative procedures and by constitutional procedures in each member state. For any of the procedures, the European Council, a decision-making body of the EU, must give its approval (Article 7(1) of the Treaty establishing the European Union). This provision means that only the EU Court of Justice can challenge the legality of an EU law before the European Council. The EU has a single budget system which is legally binding upon all EU member states.

Some remote sensing scientists have proposed using the measurement of the radiance coming from vegetation canopies in those bands to characterize plant health status from a satellite platform. This approach exploits the fact that in those bands it is possible to discriminate the vegetation's reflectance from its fluorescence, which is much weaker.

Plant physiology at the spectrum scale and in the tropics

Plants that live at higher latitudes are at greater risk from light pollution because they have fewer photosynthetic intermediaries (e.g., photosynthetic ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (PbS) reductase, the C 3, C 4 photosynthetic pathway, chloroplasts, and the enzymes that help them to capture and transfer essential carbon–carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) bonds into oxygen). In addition, the tropics are also the place where air masses are thickest. So light from the tropics may be concentrated for a much longer time, producing a greater exposure time for the plants in the tropics to increasing light levels.

As with other life processes, the tropics are also home to an extraordinary variety of organisms, a testament to the complex interactions that occur between them and their environment. A unique study (Sobel et al., 2007) found that about half of the photosynthetic intermediates detected from the tropics in the first eight weeks of the year originated in water-limited plants. This study also found that the species composition of photosynthetic intermediates in the tropics shifted significantly with increasing latitudinal latitude.

Another study (Weis et al., 2008) looked at a plant species, Z. chinensis, that lives in the northern hemisphere (in the subtropics), but which grows at elevations as high as 26,000′ (about 4,700 m, or 15,000 ft) in the tropics. Many of the reviews and comments I have read about this movie say that this is a rather stale film and performance by Clara Bow. Although the story-line was rather typical of Clara's later silents, I still find it somewhat heart-stirring and incredibly fun. Clara plays a happy-go-lucky Hawaiian girl who will stop at nothing to win the man she loves...never mind that this man is married! I remember seeing this movie and feeling a sense of nostalgia, as it was essentially the first time I saw Clara Bow act on screen. In order to accomplish the romance needed for success, Clover must be very charming, and make sure to be in full contact with the guy she's going after. By the way, her smile and easygoing nature are not faked, as she says so herself - this is the real Clara Bow! The relationship builds throughout the movie and is portrayed in a really subtle way, so that you're not too concerned about their romantic interations (though I won't deny that they are pretty damn funny).

As far as sound is concerned: for this movie, everything was recorded live (but not "recorded" - this was recorded). There are plenty of opportunities to hear Clara's voice when she's singing some wonderful songs. The movie was also meant to be a tribute to the movie "Dorothy's Daze", filmed in Hawaii by the same director and actresses. The musical motif for this movie is "Hoi Kahiu". So if you want to get a real Hawaiian girl dancing in your head, you should check this movie out.

The Bottom line: This is an entertaining, classic romantic comedy with a great story. If you're a fan of the classic Disney films then this is a must-see. If you're a fan of classic movies, you might have no reason to check out any movie except this one...but if you do, then you're bound to adore this movie just as much I did.

The aim of the uniflow is to remedy this defect and improve efficiency by providing an additional port uncovered by the piston at the end of each stroke making the steam flow only in one direction. By this means, the simple-expansion uniflow engine gives efficiency equivalent to that of classic compound systems with the added advantage of superior part-load performance, and comparable efficiency to turbines for smaller engines below one thousand horsepower. The key improvement to this design is in the way that it creates a flow through the crankcase in the direction of the port, allowing the water in the crankcase to cool down and condense before passing to the cylinder in the opposite direction. The advantage of this is that the fuel consumption can be greatly reduced and that the fuel oil can be disposed of more cleanly in the combustion chamber for reduced emissions, whilst also giving greater range, fuel economy and a reduction in fuel consumption. This arrangement does appear to be somewhat more complex in general, and requires that the main uniflow impeller are equipped with spoked main gear wheels mounted on the crankcase and supporting the main spindle which spins the main engine gear or "belt" and the smaller uniflow impeller. It is thought that decreasing levels of vitamin D may lead to impaired immune function and an increased risk of infectious diseases. The VDRs are found in a major number of tissues, including the spleen, liver, muscle, and the epithelial lining of the small intestine. VDRs exist abundantly in the spleen because, similar to Rho family members, it is the only cell that can produce them. The spleen also contains receptors and cofactors that interact with VDR's to regulate their activity through interactions with co-secretory cells. text: Buried deep within the NFL's 21 proposed rule changes were a series of suggestions that would provide what I think is much-needed roster flexibility, especially in an era that has made player safety a key emphasis and when time for player development has been squeezed.Most would entail increased costs, minor on an industry scale but a factor nonetheless, so I would bet their chances for approval aren't high. Still, this is a positive discussion and a sign that -- one day -- teams might not be as constricted as they are now. Let's run through them individually while we have a moment:Expanded game rosters: At the moment, teams must deactivate seven of their 53 players on game day. Under the rule change proposed here, an additional player can be brought on in the first quarter of a game. I'm not yet certain whether this would apply to an NFL League-wide basis, but it might be better for one team to bring on a player with a hamstring injury as opposed to having to deactivate a player with two touchdowns on a Saturday night.A team cannot use more than 22 guys on its active roster in a season. There are currently 16 roster spots available, so it's possible this rule change would reduce the number of regular-season players added to the team. In 2012, teams signed a combined 51 players to open all the way through Week 16.Under the proposed rule change, each team, instead of a player making 53 appearances, would have a maximum of 53 spots. That would have meant that, for example, a team with an active roster of 85 players needed at least nine players (eight for the practice squad, two more for the practice squad/future, and two for the practice squad/veteran) to reach the 53-man maximum. Both X.25 and Frame Relay provide connection-oriented operations. But X.25 does it at the network layer of the OSI Model. Frame Relay does it at level two, the data link layer. I have not seen Frame Relay used with a "client" layer, with the software-only operation of a standard telephone line.

The argument is an appeal to authority.

It is a fallacy, and in my opinion a weak argument. But it is one that might be useful in some organizations.

As a conclusion, we have seen the difference between the X.25 protocol itself, and which operating system packages or operating system service packages implement it. The use of applications and servers based on the X.25 protocol is not universal, and can be found only in small scale, and specific, organizations. The Standard Industrial Classification and the newer North American Industry Classification System have a classification system for companies that perform or otherwise engage in construction. To recognize the differences of companies in this sector, it is divided into three subsectors: building construction, heavy and civil engineering construction, and specialty trade contractors.

The building construction sector is divided into building components, such as the framing system, structural metal system, building assembly or floor systems, exterior wall systems, and so forth. These components are installed according to the requirements of the building's codes. These components are classified into three distinct categories. The structure component is a building that comprises the core structure of the foundation, walls, and supporting walls, and is required according to building codes to be installed. The mechanical system component consists of systems installed for power, ventilation, heating, lighting, air conditioning, and air conditioning system. The plumbing system is a structural component in the building whose purpose is to distribute, filter, and remove substances in the building such as dust, water, gases, and liquid wastes. (In contrast, the plumbing system is not installed in the construction of a house nor, for building design purposes, is the plumbing system as such considered to be part of the building) The materials system component consists of systems which serve as storage for supplies such as cement, mortar, and brick used in the construction of the building.

The heavy and civil engineering construction sector is divided into heavy construction and civil construction which includes the use the heavy equipment required for the completion of the structure. Civil construction means the use of heavy machinery used for the construction of the structure but does not include the use of heavy equipment installed in the structure but not required to be supplied by the heavy construction contractor, such as hydraulic jacks with a hand-operated hydraulic system to move walls and other structure components.

Several barriers protect organisms from infection, including mechanical, chemical, and biological barriers. The waxy cuticle of many leaves, the exoskeleton of insects, the shells and membranes of externally deposited eggs, and skin are examples of mechanical barriers that are the first line of defense against infection. However, as organisms cannot be completely sealed from their environments, other systems act to protect body openings such as the lungs, intestines, and the genitourinary tract. Chemical barriers act in the absence of pathogens to suppress pathogen growth or the spread of disease. Biological barriers restrict microbial entry, including those produced by the immune system and by species of bacteria and fungi. Bacterial, protozoan, and helminthic infections are believed to be the major causes of death in humans.

The waxy cuticle of leaves is a strong barrier, providing resistance to insects, diseases, and damage caused by chemicals. If an insect passes through the cuticle, it is unable to enter the interior of the leaf's interior, a process known as tricheinization. The outer waxy layer of the leaf also provides an area for mechanical protection when its outer leaves are destroyed. The internal layer of a woody plant is also a mechanical barrier that allows for plant growth, preventing injury to a plant without entering the plant itself.

Mechanical Barrier The cuticle of some plants acts as a mechanical barrier to direct attack by insects to the interior of the plant as well as to direct attack by fungi and bacteria to the exterior. Cuticle structure of plants includes spines, horny spines, hair, filaments, sheaths, or sheaths, and, in some cases, thorns. Overview and Clinical Applications

Almost all ctenophores are predators – there are no vegetarians and only one genus that is partly parasitic. If food is plentiful, they can eat 10 times their own weight per day. While Beroe preys mainly on other ctenophores, other surface-water species prey on zooplankton (planktonic animals) ranging in size from the microscopic, including mollusc and fish larvae, to small adult crustaceans such as copepods, amphipods, and even krill.

Life cycle

The Beroe ctenophore lives in large colonies called "soul sessons" and often lives underground in caves. The ctenophore egg consists of approximately 100,000 cells and is covered by a cell-wall-enclosed envelope. During the larval stage, the ctenophore is protected by its large-eyed mouthparts. Like most ctenophores, the egg is enclosed within a protective, silken egg capsule which allows the ctenophore to survive the short journey from a developing egg-body to the world of plankton.

The newly-hatched ctenophores undergo an additional process called oogenesis in which eggs are placed in a nest-like structure made up of fine-particles called "biofilms." Once the brood is ready to hatch, the hatchling is a bright purple-yellow-white, with greenish-pink hairs and no eyes.

Inhabits

These animals are usually found in dark, slow-moving waters. They are rarely seen by humans, though their presence can sometimes be felt as the water temperature changes. They also often occur in dense and protected swamps and estuaries where they feed on microscopic plants and zooplankton. Even in calm waters that lack ctenophores, other, smaller species live very close to the surface in groups.

This species of ctenophore occurs throughout the Indo-Pacific. It is most commonly found in the Hawaiian Islands from Hawaii and the eastern Pacific to Japan.

Although it is generally accepted that EU law has primacy, not all EU laws give citizens standing to bring claims: that is, not all EU laws have "direct effect". In Van Gend en Loos v Nederlandse Administratie der Belastingen it was held that the provisions of the Treaties (and EU Regulations) are directly effective, if they are (1) clear and unambiguous (2) unconditional, and (3) did not require EU or national authorities to take further action to implement them. Van Gend en Loos, a postal company, claimed that what is now TFEU article 30 prevented the Dutch Customs Authorities charging tariffs, when it imported urea-formaldehyde plastics from Germany to the Netherlands. (The TFEU says that the use of natural or artificial flavourings is an industrial product. The Dutch argued that to give such a right to consumers is like putting a label "CIGARETTE PEAFOAM" on a soft drink). The court held that "the word 'decided' in Articles 2 and 6 has a direct effect of guaranteeing the application of the Treaties." Article 2 also states that "only the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States shall constitute general rules of procedure for the Union." Therefore, the court held that "it was incumbent upon the parties to a decision concerning the application of the Treaty to decide, in accordance with the principles of their law, whether, at the time of the proceedings, or at a later moment when the decision was being revised under the conditions of Article 6 of the Treaty, they had the right to review the grounds and the procedure followed in drawing up the decision."

What was left for the court to decide in the case of Van Gend en Loos was the question of whether it were indeed a case of a clear and unambiguous decision or not. The court had to decide whether there was a binding EU rule regarding the taxation of goods from third countries, namely the provision in EU Regulation No. 890/2007 with its reference to "EU directives, decisions of the European Parliament and Council or the Commission concerning the implementation of EU law."

Decision problems are one of the central objects of study in computational complexity theory. A decision problem is a special type of computational problem whose answer is either yes or no, or alternately either 1 or 0. The basic strategy is to reduce a problem to its simplest possible components and then to find the decision problem for that component. If it is possible to derive a decision problem for an element, we say that element is decision-optimal. If the decision problem for a specific element is not a simple one, we say that this element is non-decision-optimal. To make a decision, an agent has to select among possible answers, as in Aeschylus' Lavinia, but the relevant element here is that the agent chooses among all possible answers to the decision problem (i.e., between 1 and 0).

Hypersensitivity is an immune response that damages the body's own tissues. They are divided into four classes (Type I – IV) based on the mechanisms involved and the time course of the hypersensitive reaction. Type I hypersensitivity is an immediate or anaphylactic reaction, often associated with allergy. Type II sensitization takes several hours to several days. Type III is also an immediate or anaphylactic reaction, most commonly associated with food allergies. Type IV hypersensitivity requires a delayed or chronic process which can be in remission or recurrent.

Why does our body react the way it does to allergens?

Our immune system is an amazing system. It contains cells with specialized receptors capable of detecting specific antigens that will initiate an immune response to the target antigens. When the immune system identifies a new or unfamiliar antigen, the body is triggered to produce the appropriate white blood cells. The immune cells recognize the new antigen as a foreign invader from the outside world.

To determine if we're experiencing a hypersensitivity reaction, we use IgE sensitization testing. It reveals the immunological characteristics of the individual. If a specific antigen or protein is recognized by the immune system but not by the test result, then we have an apparent true hypersensitivity reaction.

What are the possible side effects?

There are no known side effects of sensitization. Most people experience minor sore throats, wheezing, nasal congestion and itching at first. When these symptoms are left untreated, they often progress. If your symptoms are persistent, you may need further testing to rule out an underlying condition.

Under the Yuan dynasty, the Mongolian Empire covered the territory with about three million people, of which two millenia (or about a thousand years) of continuous rule was achieved, between the first century AD and the 13th century AD. The Mongolian empire was a powerful superpower during the Middle Ages, and at the beginning of the 17th century, it controlled four of five continents, including the United States of America and a large part of Africa, in addition to the former Mongolian Soviet Socialist Republic, which existed from 1861 to 1953. During the same period, the imperial dynasty was succeeded by two successor states. These were later unified to form the Chinese Republic of China.

Historical events [ edit ]

The Mongol Empire stretches from modern day Asia Minor in the south; Persia to the North, with the westernmost parts in modern-day Russia and Mongolia; and to the Middle East in the west. The empire reached its greatest extent between the 11th and 13th century under Kublai Khan, the first of the Mongolian Khanate of the Yuan Dynasty. I will say it's refreshing to see a film that looks a little more like a movie and less like an advertisement for a luxury product. "This is because in a lot of cultures, disabled people are regarded as 'lucky' or 'unlucky'," he explains. "So many companies don't value people with disabilities on the merit, and instead expect it through what they perceive as a 'lucky charm', so you have to go and try hard in order to win the company's trust and to become their favourite."

'Some people have no idea how to treat disabled people'

Many machine models different from the standard multi-tape Turing machines have been proposed in the literature, for example random access machines. Such machines differ from the classic Turing machines by the fact that they do not generate a set of input bits for each Turing machine step. They perform finite computations and only emit (one-way) finite streams of ones. More recently, Markov chain models have emerged in attempts to model the properties that the Turing machines exhibit in certain contexts (e.g., as a deterministic mechanism to simulate a decision tree, a model of how neurons in a brain process information).

There is currently much debate in the literature over which Turing machines are best suited to encode information in the presence of noise. For example, Bostrom and Strogatz (2006) argue that the canonical Turing machine is an interesting model, but that the canonical Turing machine in their model is defective, since it does not generate and emit a discrete set of bits, and therefore has poor capacity to model the problems of real quantum mechanical systems. Furthermore, there is debate as to whether the canonical Turing machine can be represented as a simple set of discrete values or whether the computation steps must yield discrete values on the order of 1 to the power of n, given that the input sequence in this setup is the most complex possible sequence (see Bostrom and Strogatz (2008) for a discussion of the latter argument).

A model like the C2-SAT, which allows for much finer-control over the computational steps, is another possibility for representing the world informationally. The C2-SAT model is similar to the classical Turing machine—it generates sequences of one-bit symbols such that every symbol is paired

text: When rock units are placed under horizontal compression, they shorten and become thicker. Because rock units, other than muds, do not significantly change in volume, this is accomplished in two primary ways: through faulting and folding. In the shallow crust, where brittle deformation can occur, thrust faults form, which cause deeper rock to move on top of shallower rock. This produces fractures, or fissures, or fissures of the crust, which can be easily enlarged by faults within an intervening rock unit. Where a fault can traverse, a rift will form. The thickness of rift faulting will increase with the depth to the target unit. chiari type i malformation is a tonsillar herniation more than 3 mm from the level of foramen magnum , with or without concurrent syringomyelia . In other words, the neck of the vertebral canal cannot be extended.

In the case of Chiari malformation of the cervical spine, the laminae are compressed in the area of the foramen by a congenital spinal cord lesion, and the foramen is too small to allow fusion with the vertebral canal. The lack of cervical spine fusion results in a vertebral canal that has a flat topography of the lateral (bony) wall. In the case of the Chiari malformation of the thoracic spine, the laminae are compressed by a congenital spinal cord lesion, and the foramen is too large to enable fusion with the vertebral canal. The lack of thoracic spine fusion results in a thoracic canal that has a rounded topography of the lateral wall. The difference in the topography of the lamina is due to the fact that the cervical canal has a greater curvature than the thoracic canal. Thus, the vertebral canal of Chiari malformation is more likely to result in the creation of a transverse compression-like curve than in the creation of longitudinal compression of the cervical spinal cord.

In patients with Chiari malformation, the lateral walls of the laminae can overlap the medial walls of the vertebral canal. If this region of overlap is the result of fusion with a cervical cervical disc, the patient tends to have symptoms of cervical dislocation or disc syndrome.

Pathogens can rapidly evolve and adapt, and thereby avoid detection and neutralization by the immune system; however, multiple defense mechanisms have also evolved to recognize and neutralize pathogens. Even simple unicellular organisms such as bacteria possess a rudimentary immune system, in the form of enzymes that protect against bacteriophage infections.

Bacteria are divided into different cell groups, each of which possesses a specific immune response to invading pathogens. Bacteriophage B virus (PHV), for example, recognizes specific phage genes in its host cell, then recruits specialized helper viral particles (HAVs) that engulf the phage and destroy it. However, other pathogens can circumvent phages by using protein coat proteins (PAPs) that prevent host cells from recognizing their antigens. PAPs are especially prevalent in bacteria, yeast, viruses, and fungi, and have evolved during billions of years for a variety ancillary functions such as protein packaging, membrane fusion, and assembly into larger bodies (figs. S10, S11, and S13). The PAP complex itself is made up of a set of membrane-spanning proteins (molecules that are folded into long chains) that collectively form a membrane-spanning protein framework (MFS), which surrounds the host cell (18). This MFS is composed of thousands of different proteins and is unique to each host cell and cell line. All of the members of the MFS are organized into several families of complexes, and each of these complexes contains multiple proteins that form membrane-spanning complexes (figs. S14 and S15).

Non-revolutionary civil disobedience is a simple disobedience of laws on the grounds that they are judged "wrong" by an individual conscience, or as part of an effort to render certain laws ineffective, to cause their repeal, or to exert pressure to get one's political wishes on some other issue. Revolutionary civil disobedience is more of an active attempt to overthrow a government (or to change cultural traditions, social customs, religious beliefs, etc...revolution doesn't have to be political, i.e. "cultural revolution", it simply implies sweeping and widespread change to a section of the social fabric). It may or may not include violent acts, which is a decision only the individual should make.

Revolutionary civil disobedience has a history in the United States, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It was a part of the civil rights movement in the 1950s and 60s, and during the 1980s.

In modern times revolution occurs when a revolution is forced upon a society, usually by a coup (i.e. "Arab Spring" or "Yemeni Spring"), or by political instability. However, a more extreme sort of upheaval, an extreme revolt, is considered a movement.

In the years after the Act expired at the end of 1647, a number of Huguenot families fled to New England. Some Huguenots lived under strict laws in New England and Florida before escaping again to other regions of North America and England.

The Treaty of Utrecht of 1648 abolished the religious test used to exclude Protestants from certain jobs including clergy, the military, and officials. However, the Huguenot community was also still marginalized by the political status quo. This changed in 1669 when King James II granted Huguenots the right to return to England. Their presence in England was welcomed by King Charles, who used their support in Parliament as part of his effort to undermine Protestant dominance in England. James II's wife Anne also supported Huguenots, but as both were Protestant women, she may have limited her support to the Protestant Huguenots who lived in England.

English Civil War

The English Civil War ended in 1642, when King Charles II was able to take the throne on the death of his brother Henry VIII. It was generally believed that Huguenots supported the royalists, despite them being strongly opposed to Catholicism. The English Civil War proved politically divisive and divided the English political elite between moderates, monarchists, and radicals.

Because neutrophils have the ability to be large and shed their surface membrane at will, they are called "shedding cells." They can travel hundreds of kilometers in their search for invaders.

Macrophages are specialized cells that act primarily as part of an immune network to kill invading pathogens. The macrophages are present in the body only if they are infected or injured by a pathogen. When an injury occurs, they begin to secrete a number of inflammatory factors, which cause other cells to start to secrete pro-inflammatory cells and protein. The result is a chain reaction that leads to tissue destruction. The immune system normally consists of multiple types of cells, each with a functional role in various stages of the immune response. However, the immune cells play a vital role in helping the body fight off infections.

In addition to these, human cells are able to replicate and make antibodies to fight foreign invaders. Pro-inflammatory immune cells called eosinophils have been described as "white blood cells capable of recognizing and destroying foreign invaders." current and upcoming surveys will measure the cosmological parameters with an extremely high accuracy . the primary goal of these observations is to eliminate some of the currently viable cosmological models created to explain the late time accelerated expansion ( either real or only inferred ) . however , most of the statistical tests used in cosmology have a strong requirement : the use of a model to fit the data . in contrast, the observed cosmic parameters are not well constrained to a model at the present time. this is a unique opportunity to analyze the cosmological parameters without a specific cosmological theory.
